conserved_row.complete_before_row: 2.2 Fix a Euclidean metric in one link chart and transport it through the similarity charts. The metric is independent of the transport path, because every loop has identity linear holonomy and translations preserve the Euclidean metric. This gives a global flat metric $g_v$ on the compact torus $T_v$, hence a complete one. Its lift to the universal cover is complete as well: any geodesic projects to a geodesic on the complete torus, extends there, and the extension lifts through the covering. The lifted Euclidean charts develop to a local isometry into $\mathbb R^2$. Every finite straight segment starting at a point in the image lifts to its endpoint: a partial lift has finite length, is therefore Cauchy, and extends from its limit by the local isometry. Hence the development is onto. For a small Euclidean ball about any point, lifting its radial segments from each preimage gives disjoint isometric copies of that ball; lifting the reverse radial segments shows these copies exhaust its preimage. Thus the development is a covering, and since $\mathbb R^2$ is simply connected it is an isometry. Deck transformations have identity linear part by the trivial link holonomy, so act by translations. Compactness of $T_v$ makes their translation vectors a rank-two lattice $\Lambda_v$. The assembled end is therefore the quotient of a horoball by $\Lambda_v$, with metric $dr^2+e^{-2r}g_v$ in horospherical depth $r$. A path escaping toward the ideal vertex has length at least the change in $r$, so the end is complete. Repeating this argument at each of the finitely many vertices proves completeness at every end. This is the local cusp argument underlying [F3], carried out separately on every link; the one-vertex Statement of [F3] is not applied to the full triangulation.
